name: Agent: Video Production
summary: Turns a brief into finished social video — the footage, the edit, the music, the voice-over, the captions — with a person approving before anything costs money.
objectives: Finished video straight from Claude: footage, edit, music, voice-over, captions and quality checks in one run.
The best quality for the lowest cost.
Ten to thirty social videos per campaign, as themed versions of one main video.
Add a new brand by adding a folder. The agent itself never changes.
Nothing that costs money runs until a person says go.

outcomes.text: It made a full campaign: one main video and three themed versions, each in two languages and three shapes, with captions burned in and a subtitle file per language. A person approved every step.

The cheap check caught the expensive mistake. A generated image came back with broken English written on it — in an ad for an English school. It was thrown out at the sketch stage, for the price of a picture instead of the price of a finished video.

Every cost is checked before it is spent, recorded job by job, and matched afterwards against the provider's own receipt. A cost the provider never reports gets marked as missing, instead of quietly counted as zero.

Using it for real found four faults in the agent itself — music that never actually got mixed in, a version that inherited the wrong voice-over. Each one became a fix, plus a test that fails if it ever comes back.
The quality check now checks itself. It used to report all-clear while running one of the four checks it promised. The videos were fine; the all-clear was not worth much until this was fixed.

One thing it has not done yet: generate its own footage. The campaign it made end to end used client material that was already shot and silent, so the AI generation, the two languages and the native-speaker review have never all run on one real job.

That run is the next step and it is deliberately gated: a real brief, a person's go-ahead, and a ceiling of 100 credits. Until it happens, the agent is proven as a pipeline and unproven as a producer.

Every price it quotes was checked against the real account, and three were wrong. A quote is a floor, not a forecast: one job quoted at 22 credits cost 90. And a plan feature called "unlimited" is real only in a browser — the agent uses another door, where it still pays.

The music rule was strict in a way that made no sense: it refused a properly licensed track for the sole reason that a machine made it. The test is now the licence, confirmed by a person. What did not change is the part that bites: no recorded licence, no music — the video ships silent and says why.

Dubbing into another language was costed from a guess of about 100 credits. The two real jobs on record cost 121 and 142 — so one language alone would eat a third of the budget set aside for an entire test campaign. It is written down as priced and not yet available, rather than quietly offered.

The model list can now be refreshed by a command that shows what changed and waits for approval. It edits single lines instead of rewriting the file, because most of that file explains why each price is what it is — and it stops rather than guess when a model appears or disappears.

The intake form was rebuilt around how a campaign is actually run, not just where it gets published. One question — "which channel?" — turned out to be three: what kind of video, how it gets made, and where it ships. Nine parts of the system depend on the third meaning, so it kept its name.

The form now offers things the agent cannot yet do — TV ads, two editing tools, brand characters — and marks each one instead of hiding it. The request gets recorded; the run gets blocked. Asking for something we cannot build yet is useful information, not a mistake to reject.

It will not render a language nobody agreed to review. Open English ships to four markets and two are Spanish — Latin America and Spain are different copy read by different people, so they count as two. Spain and Turkey have no reviewer yet, so both are blocked.

Review texts can now be sent to the reviewer by Slack, a shared document, or email. Sending is not approving: the video stays blocked until that person's sign-off is actually written down, for every language separately.
Every finished file now lands in one folder named after the ticket that asked for it, so a delivery can be traced back to its request without anyone remembering a naming rule.

The form used to carry one brand's settings inside the shared agent, which meant adding a brand required editing the tool. Those settings moved out to the brand's own folder, and the shared form now refuses to open without one rather than showing an empty page that looks like it works.

Text now sits where the platform leaves room for it, by construction rather than by eye. Every caption, logo and on-screen line is placed from one written-down set of margins — so the layout and the check that grades it cannot disagree.

Three of the six layouts could not be described the old way at all. YouTube's top edge is a staircase, not a straight line, and flattening it would have thrown away about a fifth of the usable width of every wide video.
The social layout has a column of buttons covering only the lower half of the screen. Treating that as a permanent margin would have surrendered space that is free everywhere above it.

The quality gate used to answer a smaller question than people read into it: it confirmed a layout existed for the target platform, never that anything was inside it. Those are now two checks, and the second fails a batch when a caption or logo strays.

Square and portrait-crop layouts have no official reference yet, so they are marked provisional and every review still is stamped PROVISIONAL. A guess and a measurement should never look the same to whoever approves the work.

A video cut for one shape is not automatically safe in another — the square version crops the top off the tall one. Positions are now worked out against every shape a campaign ships, and checked again separately for each.

The tool that keeps platform specs current can no longer overwrite the official layouts; it proposes and stops. As it was, one approved refresh would have deleted forty lines explaining why those numbers are what they are.

Eleven safeguards were each deliberately broken on a scrap copy to confirm the tests catch them. Eleven for eleven — and the harness refuses to count a crashed test as a test that caught something, which is how its own first run turned out to be false alarms.

The brief form now works from a link, so anyone can fill one in without a copy of the repo. It ships empty: you load your own project's settings in your browser, and they never leave your machine. The page has no way to send them anywhere, and the browser is what enforces that.

Getting it ready to publish found the form was quietly carrying things that belong to us: what two real jobs cost on our account, two supplier names, an internal chat channel, a real ticket number. Not secret exactly — and all of it would have been on a public page.

So there is now a check that reads the projects folder and refuses to publish if anything from it — a client name, a person's name, a shared link, a brand colour — has been typed into the shared form. Add a client and the check covers them without anyone remembering.
That check caught its own author twice: once flagging a comment written while explaining the rule, and once, after being committed, flagging itself.

The form was rebuilt around what a choice will cost. A list down the side shows what still has to be fixed and, separately, what will stop the video being made — because asking for something we cannot build yet is worth recording, not rejecting.

All thirty option buttons were unreachable by keyboard and invisible to a screen reader, and no field had a proper label. Both fixed. Colours are now measured for whatever brand is loaded, which found a selected option whose label had always been below the legibility line.

The narrow-screen check had been passing on a picture rather than a layout: the preview tool cannot go below a certain width, so a phone-sized screenshot was really a crop of a desktop one. Measured properly, the page ran 473 pixels off the side of a phone. It does not now.
The form is published and working — anyone on the team opens a link, with no copy of the repository.

It was checked against the page as served, not against the intention: what the address hands back is byte for byte the file that was reviewed, it comes up empty as it should, and an attempt to send data out is refused by the browser itself.
What used to be shared was a different file that only worked inside Claude's own chat, and was already two days out of date. That route never worked for a publishable version; the link replaces it.

The published link was still unusable by the people it was for: it opened on a file chooser asking for a settings file that lives in a private repository. It now opens straight on the brand's own form, carrying a stripped-down copy of those settings.
What may be published is a list of what is allowed, not a list of what is banned — so a field added to the settings later stays off the page unless somebody adds it on purpose.

Reviewer names, voice-talent names, shared links and past spending are not on that page. Not as a promise: the build refuses to write itself if any of them appears, and it names everything it dropped every time it runs.

The form now sends itself. One button files the brief straight into a shared folder and emails whoever runs the agent, instead of downloading a file somebody has to forward. If sending fails the download button comes back, with the reason.
A filled-in form is never lost — the worst outcome available is the behaviour it had yesterday, plus an explanation of why.

Leaving out the delivery folder — correct, because a share link hands out access — quietly made the published form impossible to submit, since that same field is one the form refuses to open without. Every test passed. Only opening it in a browser showed it.

The fix follows a distinction the agent already had: a missing folder is unassigned, not wrong. The form accepts it, the run stays blocked until it is filled, and it gets filled from the brand's own settings when the request is taken in.
Chasing that also turned up an older contradiction nobody had hit: the rules promised an empty field the operator would fill, and then rejected exactly that.

The form now sends itself. One button files the brief straight into a shared folder and emails whoever runs the agent, instead of downloading a file somebody has to forward. If sending fails for any reason the download button comes back, with the reason — a filled-in form is never lost.

The shared form still cannot send anything anywhere. The sending code sits there switched off and the browser is what enforces it: only a published build for one brand gets a destination, and only the one it was built with.

Taking a submitted brief in is now one command: it files the campaign, fills in the delivery folder, runs every check, and says plainly whether it can run or what is blocking it. It moves no approval — every point where money is spent is still a person saying go.
A check written to stop the page sending data anywhere but the one approved address turned out to accept the exact trick it was written to stop. Its own test caught that the first time it ran.

The tool that proves the safeguards work was itself proving the wrong thing: five of its checks were passing for an unrelated reason, so they were not testing what they claimed. Fixed — and one safeguard was deleted rather than kept, because it could no longer fail at all.
The endpoint is live. A brief filled on the public page now files itself into the team's Drive folder and emails whoever runs the agent — verified from the live page, not from a copy of it.

Getting there found that the design's own requirement was not on offer: the company Google account blocks apps that anyone can reach, so the option simply is not in the menu, and the restricted version refuses the form with a sign-in page.
So the receiving end runs from a separate account that has permission to write into one folder and nothing else. The briefs stay in the company Drive; the folder is never shared with anyone.

The setup guide's own test command was wrong in a way that looked exactly like a broken endpoint — it reported an error for an hour while the thing had been working the whole time. Corrected, with the reason written down.
Every refusal was made to refuse before trusting it: a token with one character changed, no token at all, an old document version, and a brief with no ticket number. Four for four.

The form now asks one section at a time, with the list down the side working as tabs and a summary at the top naming what is still required. Somebody filling one in reads what is left instead of scrolling a wall of questions.

Nothing still to fill in is coloured as a mistake. An unfinished form is not an error, and the one colour reserved for errors is now used nowhere in it — what stops the video being made is marked, in its own colour, separately from what is merely unanswered.

The brand typeface had never loaded, for anyone, in any version — and two of our own documents said it had. It stayed invisible because the machine doing the checking already had the font installed. It is written down as not working, instead of left looking as though it did.

The redesign reached the link the team actually opens. That is a separate act from finishing it: the page had been serving the previous design, and publishing is a step a person takes on purpose — nothing here pushes to a public page by itself.

The agent was audited against its own written rules for the first time — by a separate tool that reads what the documents promise and then goes looking for the code that keeps the promise. Fifteen faults, each pinned to a line.

The form that takes a brief and the part that turns it into a video have stopped speaking the same language. The form now writes the newer format; the builder reads only the older one; the step that takes briefs in refuses anything else. Nothing joins them.
The tests did not notice, because the only test of that step feeds it a brief in the old format. A green suite over a shape the system no longer produces is the exact thing an audit is for.

A rule the documents state twice — that a voice may not be used in a language nobody has listened to — is enforced by nothing. The file named as doing it is called by no running part. The check that does run asks about the reviewer of the text: another question.

Two of the fifteen stop work and get their own session, each fix graded by breaking it again to prove the test notices. Eight are written down to be fixed when that area is next touched. Five are noted and nothing more. The audit suggests and never edits — not one file of the agent was changed.

Both are now fixed. The builder reads the newer brief format, so a brief filed through the public form can finally become a video. Declaring the older format the only supported one was rejected: there is no other way in, so it would have retired the template feature rather than drawn a line.

Three things a newer brief can say are now refused rather than guessed at: an unresearched platform, an unknown one, and a screen shape with no dimensions. Each guess would have made a video that looked correct, was not what was asked for, and passed every later check.

The rule that a voice may not speak a language nobody has heard it speak is now enforced in code, in both brief formats. It was stated in two places and implemented in none — the check that did run asks who reviewed the written text, a different question about a different person.

Language codes are matched exactly, on purpose. Letting a Spain request inherit a Latin-America approval would claim a voice was checked for a market where nobody has listened to it — the precise substitution the rule exists to prevent.

It immediately stopped a test campaign that had been passing: it names a voice, and its brand folder has no voice file at all, so nobody can say that voice was ever heard. Record the listen, or drop the voice. Writing an approval nobody earned is not an option.

Each fix was graded by breaking it again on a scrap copy and requiring the test to fail — and both were graded on the wiring, not the function, because both faults were correct code that nothing called. Thirty-six safeguards now prove they can go red, up from thirty-two.

The brief form now asks which voice will speak the ad, and shows whether anyone has actually heard that voice in each language chosen. Before this, the rule existed in code but the form collected no voice, so nothing could ever trigger it.

Two separate warnings, because they are two different people: one asks whether a native speaker reviewed the written script, the other whether anyone has listened to the voice in that language. Neither answers for the other.
Language codes are matched exactly. A Latin-America approval does not carry over to Spain — same language, different market, different listen — and a test now breaks if that shortcut is ever taken.
The published form was hiding the fact that decides the outcome: the voice status was stripped out before publishing. It now travels, while the voice talent's name and the provider's id still do not.

Taking in a brief now refuses one that belongs to a different brand. The form is public and per-brand, so a download folder holding two brands' briefs is normal — filing the wrong one used to succeed quietly and put the files in the wrong place.

Checked in a real browser, not only in tests: the picker renders, the status changes with the languages chosen, and the warning appears and disappears with it. This form once shipped impossible to submit with every test green.

Open English now has its first reusable video template — and it is not a new idea: it is the campaign that already shipped, written down. Eight videos, four approvals, fifteen credits. The only structure here that is proven rather than designed.

Writing it down was blocked by a fault nobody could see. A beat could have footage, or it could have words and a voice, but not both — so the one campaign this thing has actually made could not be expressed as a template at all.

It failed silently, which is worse: you wrote a shot into the template and got a blank card back, no error, from the part whose whole job is to refuse loudly. A scene's type now says who may change it, and nothing about whether it may have a picture.

The template names no model. It describes the shot and lets the current price list choose — a model name written into a brand's file is a price frozen on the day someone typed it, and three of those have already turned out wrong here.
A template lives in two files: one the builder reads, one the brief form reads. They are now compared on every run, down to each scene's type, because that type is what the cost estimate prices.
That check found a test template on its first run that existed but was in nobody's picker. Nothing was broken — it just could never have been chosen.

A campaign that shipped named a voice that does not exist — through eight videos, four approvals and a reconciled invoice. Chasing it found why nobody noticed: the part that attaches the audio never read that field at all.

So the field said who speaks the ad, and nothing checked it. It does now: the voice has to be one the brand has recorded, or a stand-in the price list knows about. Anything else stops the mix, and every run names the voice it used.

Only one of the eleven entries on record was actually wrong. The rest were honest and stayed as they were — one campaign really was made with a stand-in voice, and renaming it would have recorded something that did not happen.

The same file's other safeguard, meant to stop one version's soundtrack landing on another version's picture, was matching names loosely enough to let a shorter name pass for a longer one — and to reject a correct pair whose name had a capital letter in it.
That file had no tests at all, which is how both faults survived. It has them now, including a sweep over every campaign on record checking that each one names a voice that can actually be found.

The whole machine then ran end to end at zero cost, on the campaign that already shipped: twelve files rendered, voiced and mixed with today's code. The voice was bound and named, the music licence was checked, and every quality check that could run passed.

The quality gate still refused to sign it — the old campaign names no platform, so the layout checks could not be asked, and this gate does not turn "never asked" into "approved". New briefs name their platforms, so a real campaign gets asked everything.
What remains unproven is exactly one thing: generating new footage with paid AI. That is the next milestone — a real brief, a spending cap, and a person saying go.

One of the four things the form offered but could not make is now made. Motion graphics — animated text, numbers, logo stings, branded transitions, no filmed or generated footage — runs on the editing tool the agent already had. No new supplier, no new bill.

The plan for it was built on a belief that turned out to be false, and checking first is what caught it. The job was written as "let people pick this tool for that kind of video". They already could. Nothing had ever been linked to anything.

What was actually broken was the shape of the question. The form asks two things — what kind of video, and which tool — and the agent checked them separately. So one kind was refused whichever tool you paired it with, and the pairing that works could never be reached.

It now checks the pair. Two combinations run today and the other ten are refused by name, so a brief asking for one buildable thing and one unbuildable thing is told which is which. Before, it named a single word and left you guessing whether the rest was fine.

Turning one thing on must not quietly turn on another. Every one of the twelve combinations is now tested individually, and one test deliberately removes the new permission at run time to confirm the refusal comes back — otherwise the tests only describe the code instead of holding it to anything.

Six animation pieces were built, and none of them may contain a colour, a typeface or a name belonging to any brand — those all arrive from the brand's own folder. The check that enforces this used to cover two files and now covers the whole set.

It failed on its first real run, on two comments written minutes earlier that mentioned a client by name. That is the check working: the sentence had been in the rules for a year with nothing behind it.

Two of the pieces were unreadable and only rendering them showed it. Emphasising a number by painting it in the brand's accent colour puts it on whatever contrast that colour happens to have. The text is plain now and the accent underlines it instead.

A campaign made this way costs nothing to generate, and that is measured rather than assumed — no supplier is contacted at any point. The electricity and the machine time are real and nobody meters them, so they are recorded as unknown instead of as zero.

The sketch stage got stronger rather than weaker. For generated footage a sketch is a cheap stand-in for something expensive. Here the sketch is drawn by the same code as the finished video, from the same settings — there is nothing to preview, it is the thing.

The test run found a hole in the one rule this agent will not bend. A video like this has no voice-over, and the agent read the list of languages off the voice-over — so it would have made an ad with Spanish on screen that no Spanish speaker had ever been asked to read, and reported nothing wrong.

A campaign is now in every language it speaks or writes, defined once and read by both the part that renders and the part that demands the sign-off. If those two ever disagreed, the difference would be exactly one language going out unreviewed.

The cost record quietly reported a campaign as free. Entries written with the wrong field names were accepted, counted as nothing, and totalled as a confident zero — the one thing the rule about unknown costs exists to prevent. Written down to fix, not fixed here.

The public form was rebuilt and republished with the new option live. The rebuild nearly shipped a page that could no longer send anything — the send address is not stored in the shared file and has to be passed in each time. Caught by comparing against what was already published.

The first video asked of it that is almost entirely product screens: a three-minute tour of the platform. The rule from the pilot holds without argument — screens get recorded, never generated. A generated one once came back with broken English written inside an advert for an English school.

Checking the proposed running order against the machine, rather than reading it, found three errors. It claimed one more scene and one more shot than it listed. Its timings left a two-second hole. And its recipe for a one-minute cut leaves two minutes nineteen, not one minute.

The most useful discovery was a limit, not a feature: a clip cannot be trimmed. It always plays from its own beginning and is cut off when the moment ends. So every recording has to arrive already cut to the exact length of the moment it fills, and that one fact is the first line of the shot list.

That limit then designed the one-minute version. Its recorded moments keep the exact lengths they have in the long one, so the same three files serve both videos and nothing is filmed twice. Only the drawn parts are re-timed, because those are code and cost nothing to change.

Only one of the six animated pieces can be drawn over moving footage; the other five replace the picture entirely. So every on-screen label sits on that one, rather than as a full-width headline across the middle of the screen the tour exists to show.

A statistics piece reads its number out of its own wording. Written as first proposed, the counter would have ticked up to 24 and left the rest of the phrase trailing behind it. Rewritten before anything was made, and the proof is a picture of it counting to the right number.
Nine of the twenty-one moments were drawn and reviewed today, at no cost, before a single recording exists. Whoever approves the look can approve most of it now instead of after the filming.

Those pictures also settled an argument nobody was having: the opening and closing brand marks came back as a plain ring. That is the honest signal it was built to give — nobody has supplied the logo file, and the tool is forbidden from inventing something that looks close enough.

The quality gate will not sign this one off, and that is right. A product tour names no social platform, so the layout checks cannot be asked at all — and this gate does not turn "never asked" into "approved". Four of its six checks apply and must pass; the other two get recorded as not applicable.

A second edit of the same campaign was invisible to the checker for one turn, because it routes files to a rulebook by their name and this one had a name nothing matched. It passed while never having looked. Renamed, and written down so the next person does not repeat it.

What is missing is named rather than worked around: twelve recordings, a ticket number, the reviewer's signature actually written down, the logo file, and music whose licence a person has confirmed. The one licensed track on file is a fifty-three-second rock cue written for a ten-second advert.

The first real brief came in through the published link and became a finished video. Everything up to now was the pipeline proving itself on old material; this is the first time a request arrived from outside and money was spent on it.

The brief did not describe the video it pointed at. It asked for a full-body arm dance in a busy office; the reference clip is a man sitting at a laptop at night moving his hands, followed by a branded end card. Three sketches had already been drawn from the words before anyone noticed.

A cheap draft caught it. Before committing to the expensive version, one low-resolution pass was run purely to test whether the motion could be copied at all — it could, and it also showed what the reference actually was. That draft cost a quarter of what the wrong finished video would have.

The framing was then taken from the reference itself rather than described to a model: a frame was lifted out of the original clip and only the person in it was changed. Matching the camera stopped being something a sentence had to achieve and became a property of the input.

The end card was not rebuilt. It is the brand's own finished card, already aired, cut from the reference and re-used as a stored asset — so the campaign introduces no new wording, and the question of who reviews new copy does not arise.

One sketch was thrown out because both of the character's hands read as an obscene gesture. It was technically perfect and passed every automated layout check. That is the case for keeping a person at that gate.

Quoting the price of what is actually being sent, rather than the cheapest version of the same model, made the estimate match the invoice exactly for the first time. The brief's own estimate had been four and a half times too low.
The budget ceiling could finally be checked at all. The limit is in dollars, the spending is in credits, and nothing anywhere converted between them — the rate had to be read from the live account.

Asking for the character to look like he was enjoying himself cost more than the ceiling allowed. It was not quietly absorbed: the two options were priced, put to a person, and the higher one only ran after they raised the limit for this one job. The standing limit was left where it was.

The finished master was clipping — loud enough to distort — and the quality gate passed it. The gate asks for a ceiling on peaks and then reads only the loudness number back, leaving the answer to its own question unread in the same response.

It was caught by measuring the file instead of trusting the report, then reproduced on a second, independent mix — the same numbers to the decimal. That rules out a one-off and points at the mixing step itself, which still has the fault.

Three faults in the agent were found by using it on this one job, each written down with the exact commands that reproduce it. Two of them are gates that report success without ever asking their question.

The one rule this agent will not bend was only reachable by campaigns that speak. A video made of animated text has no voice-over, so the check that a native speaker read the words never ran — and Spanish on screen was cleared to render unread. It now runs on every language spoken or written.

Worse than lenient, it was unreachable: the sign-off had nowhere to be written down. It lived inside the voice-over section, so a campaign with no voice had no field for the one thing the check closes on. It now has its own place, and one reader looks in both.

Two more had the same shape. The check that a closing card exists in every language was also hung off the voice, so a text-only campaign had nothing checked and reported what a fully covered one reports. A check that cannot run now says so, instead of passing.

And the builder demanded a spoken script for a language that only ever appears in writing, refusing work the checker had already cleared. Words are owed in every language; a script only in the ones somebody says out loud.

Tried against the real brief that came in this week rather than a test one, the fix turns out not to reach the people filling the form: the published page never asks for on-screen text, so the check still finds no language to demand a signature for.

That campaign shipped correct text because a person noticed and wrote the decision down. The next one gets the same silence, so it is recorded beside its twin — the same check is also blind to videos written by hand. Both routes are unguarded and must be fixed together.

The whole shared engine was audited a second time — every script and everything they read, in batches, with each claim run rather than reasoned. Twenty-one new faults. The audit itself changed nothing: not one file of the agent was edited.

The rule this agent will not bend is enforced on one of the four ways a job can get in. And nothing in the engine can write the answer down: the sign-off it waits for has no producer anywhere, so the only way to record one is a person editing the file by hand.

The oldest brief format has nowhere to put that sign-off at all — not skipped, impossible. That is a third unguarded route beside the two already written down, and it settles the argument about how seriously to take them.

The loudness check cannot tell silence from a measurement that never happened, and reports the second. Proved by taking the measuring tool away: it still returned all-clear, at full coverage, on a number that does not exist.

The music rule is one word wide. A track whose licence reads "NO RIGHTS" gets mixed — the check refuses only an empty field or the exact word "unverified". A person typing anything at all satisfies the strictest rule this agent has.

And when a video has no voice-over, the refusal is silent. That is exactly the shape of the newest thing the agent can do, so the kind of campaign most likely to run next is the one that cannot tell you its music was refused.

Five of the six animation pieces throw away footage the system fetched, paid for, and reported as used. The estimate quotes those shots at nothing, so the money is spent against a ceiling that cannot see it.

The subtitle file and the burned-in captions are timed by different arithmetic and drift a quarter of a second apart over a short video. Nothing compares them, because the quality gate never opens the subtitle file.

Four faults were pulled out of "fix it when you are next in there". That queue is for faults you can work around, and a fault nobody can see has none — a note you cannot know to look up is not a delay, it is an omission with a date on it.

Everything open is now one ordered plan: forty-five items, ten faults, fourteen changes, in three blocks. One earns its own session, three follow it immediately, the rest wait until somebody is in that file anyway.

The rule this agent will not bend — a native speaker approves every translated line before anything renders — was asked on only one of the four ways a video can start, and there was nowhere to write the approval down. Now every route asks, and approving is a command that records who and when.
No approval was invented for work already delivered. Videos made before this cannot be re-rendered until someone actually signs them off, which is the point: a record nobody wrote is not a review.
The music rights check was one word wide: a track labelled "NO RIGHTS" would have been mixed into an ad, and so would "pending" or "ask legal". It only ever refused a blank field.
It now accepts a recorded clearance and refuses everything else — including a genuine clearance written as a sentence, because a sentence is not something a machine can check.

The loudness check could not tell a measurement it never took from a measurement of silence, and reported the second: with the audio tool missing, a file passed every check on a number that did not exist.

A rights note on a campaign that already shipped was deliberately left unconfirmed: it was signed the same day someone corrected which file it referred to, and nothing says which came first. That campaign re-renders without music until a person listens to the track.

Closing footage could be generated, paid for, filed and then never drawn in a single frame, while the run reported it as resolved. The kinds of scene that can show a clip are now written down and checked against the code that draws them.
Half of one fix had quietly landed a month earlier — but a real fault sat in the same place, where sound was flattened on the way to disk before anything measured it.
A test written to prove one of the new checks works was rejected by the tool that grades tests: the check could not fail on its own. It was deleted rather than propped up.

The spending record wrote down whatever it was handed. An entry with the wrong field names counted as no spend at all, so two real charges became a confident "this campaign cost nothing". It now refuses an entry it cannot read.
A reconciliation survived new spending: the file said 40.5 credits had been checked against the invoice when only 3 ever had. Any new charge now cancels the claim until someone checks again.

Work could run on a model the catalogue deliberately refuses to use, and nothing between that decision and the bill noticed. The exclusion was a sentence in a comment; it is data a check can read now.
Nothing had ever read a written spending record against its own rules. The first run of that check found one invalid for weeks — and caught the project's own test writing the same kind of entry.
The reason this work was blocked turned out to be a comment describing a fault fixed six days earlier. Nobody had re-measured the file. A comment in the code is not evidence; only the measurement is.

One campaign still claims it spent no dollars and nobody has opened the provider's account to check. Left open deliberately, with the exact time windows to look in — the likely answer is not the same as a verified one.

Eight faults from the second audit are closed. The estimate no longer quotes a scene at zero because of a suggestion nobody confirmed; subtitles and picture no longer drift apart; a review copy can no longer be delivered as the ad.

A missing clip used to render as a flat colour block and pass every check with a clean exit. The person running it now says which stage they are in, so "not generated yet" and "the file is gone" stop looking identical.

One campaign's claim that it spent no dollars was checked against both providers' accounts and is true. The method is written down: the account is shared, so usage has to be attributed by API key, not by date.

The dominant fault in this audit was not the wrong check — it was the check that never runs. Four of them: one that could not fail, one no test drove, a filter matching nothing, and two entries kept open by a note nobody re-read.
All four report exactly what a healthy system reports: green, silence, pass. Every one was found by running something rather than reading it — which is the part worth carrying to the next review.

The agent's own portability check looked at two files and said so; it looks at a hundred and fifty-three now. A person's name in a note is a record of who measured what; the same name in data is something a copy carries to the next client.

Every check this agent has now runs by itself. There were 165 of them and not one ran unless somebody typed the command, so 'it passed' meant 'a person said it passed'. They run on every change now and answer in five minutes without anyone asking.

Switching them on found two more checks that had been reporting a pass without doing the work — one decided by whether a program happened to be installed on that particular laptop, the other reporting a clean search of a list it had never managed to read. Both say so now.

One gap stayed open and is written down rather than papered over: the account's plan cannot stop a failing change from being merged, only show that it failed. That last step is still a person reading the result.

The form asked for a brief; the pipeline needed a build; nothing joined them. Every field the assembly step reads was one the form never asked for, so a request picking a template could not become a video at all.

It was found by comparing what the form sends against what the pipeline opens — not by a test. The tests were green throughout, because each half was checked against a made-up example of what the other was supposed to send.

The fix splits them. The form collects what the requester knows; a second step adds what the video needs — template, shot type per slot, the words on screen in each language. Without it a request is recorded and refused a render.

The budget limit turned out never to have been checked. Two documents had promised since the start that spending was compared against it before any money moved, and no code did the comparison. It does now.

The list of a brand's stored clips had been failing its own rules for two and a half weeks and nothing could say so. The checker routes each file to a rulebook by its name, and this kind of file was on no route — so it was skipped, silently, while the run reported all-clear.

It is on a route now, which is the half that mattered. The same lesson had already been written down once, after a cost record went unchecked in exactly this way: a kind of document nobody routes is a kind of document nothing checks.

The fault itself was fixed the way this project had already argued for the identical fault one file over — widen the rule to permit the note, rather than delete the notes. They record where each clip came from, and that is the part worth keeping.

Four fields were written down as dead and due for deletion. One was not. Running the form's output through every branch showed it produced in all of them, and in all three real requests on file — deleting it would have made live documents invalid. The record was wrong, not the field.

The other three are gone, and the difference between them is written down rather than left for the next reader. Two make a document invalid if it carries them, which is a real thing to undo the day those features exist. The third changes nothing and was only ever a promise on paper.

A fault recorded as settled still read "open" directly beneath its own closing note, and the agent's manual contradicted itself about it two paragraphs apart. Both corrected. A stale record is a confident wrong answer, which is the thing writing faults down exists to avoid.

The same false claim sat in a third document, a sealed approval record, and was left unmarked because sealed records are not edited. Wrong call, made in the same commit that handled it correctly elsewhere. Sealed protects the text, not the reader.

The original sentence still stands word for word, with a dated note beneath it saying what is false, how it was measured, and what about the decision it records is still true. Nobody landing on that page now learns something untrue about today's code.

The project had no file for lessons from corrections, though the workspace has required one all along — it exists in one project of eight. Created, and deliberately not backfilled: invented entries would put false history in the one file whose worth is being true.

The confirmation you must type to skip the cheap-sketch approval was enforced only in the web page. Briefs arrive from a public form, so a request could arrive with that protection already removed and nothing would notice. It is checked now where the request is read.

The check that every reused clip and logo actually exists was called by nothing at all: a working function wired to no one, while the manual listed it in the run that happens before any money is spent. It runs there now, and a test fails if either check is unhooked again.

A music track had been held back on a campaign that already shipped: the rights were confirmed, but on the same day a mix-up over which file it was got corrected, so no document could say which track the confirmation described. Somebody listened to it. That was the only thing that could settle it.

Five entries in the project fault log described faults that had already been fixed, one for five days. A log that describes closed faults sends the next session to redo finished work, so each was checked against the code and closed with the date it had been wrong from.

The subtitle setting offered a mode the pipeline never delivered: choosing clean video plus a separate subtitle file quietly produced burned-in captions instead. The promise is withdrawn rather than the feature faked — and building it turned out to be four files of work, not one.

The brief offered a list of numbers the agent had invented — nobody at the brand had ever picked one. Marketing's real list arrived, organised by where a video is published. The form now asks that way, and falls back to the kind of video only for the ones that go nowhere public.
A product tour had no numbers, because it is not published anywhere. Three were written with the person who owns the goal — and marked unconfirmed until the product can actually count them.
One of those rules is worth keeping: leave 'no time' among the cancellation reasons as a check. A tour cannot fix that one, so if it falls too, the tour was not the cause.

The first brief sent from the real form started its run and stopped dead: it checked that the brand folder existed before downloading anything, so it was looking at an empty machine and could never have passed. Fixed the same day, with a test that reads the order of the steps.

A run reported that it had filed the brief, then stopped because the brief was not there — both lines in the same log. It had been counting the files it read, not the ones it saved. A step that saved nothing now says so.

One switch controlled two things: writing the paperwork, which is free, and spending money. The automatic run must refuse it — so it refused the paperwork too, and could never reach its own check. Two switches now. Only one costs anything.

A run that stopped used to leave nothing behind. The note saying where it stopped was written only when the run finished cleanly — the one case nobody needs it. It is written every time now, and the failed run is the one that keeps it.

The first unattended run stopped before spending anything, and the reason mattered more than the run: the campaign asked for no shot at all. It now asks for one, and the plan for the paid run says so out loud.

The spending limit is now checked in both units. Published in dollars, computed in credits, it quietly reported "not applicable" on the account with no dollar price. Converted at a real top-up price, it would already have caught one overspend.
The first authorised paid run stopped before spending, and the refusal was correct. The reason we first recorded for it was not: we said the provider had withdrawn a model, and it had not.

That question can now be asked on its own, and is asked weekly: one command reads the provider's live catalogue and reports where our own record disagrees — what left, what appeared, what changed price. It never edits the record; a person does.

The new catalogue check produced a false alarm on its first real use: it read nothing back and reported every model as withdrawn. Acting on it would have deleted our whole record of what the provider offers.

An empty answer is now treated as a failed read rather than an empty catalogue, in the check and in the cost gate that stands in front of every payment — where the same flaw was blaming a missing model for a read that never worked.

Nothing had been withdrawn. The provider changed the shape of its answer, and every tool read the models it could no longer name as models that no longer existed — then reported that as fact. A list it cannot identify is now refused outright.

The provider's catalogue turned out to be intact: every model we rely on is still there, at the same price. What had moved was the shape of the answer, and the record now carries both shapes with the date each was seen.

Reading that catalogue no longer ends with a person retyping prices out of a log into the file that prices the work. The tool writes the reading; a person still decides what it means before anything is recorded.
